conventions: Body maps: north is at the top and east longitude increases to the right. centerLongitudeDeg is the east longitude at the image centre (null = unknown or not meaningful). For a point at east longitude L and latitude B: u = 0.5 + (L - centerLongitudeDeg) / 360 (modulo 1, from the left edge), v = (90 - B) / 180 (from the top edge). latitudeType says which latitude B is: 'planetocentric' or 'planetographic'. The two types differ for a flattened body only. An entry with no latitudeType has no statement of the source about it. Where a longitude note says 'found by inspection' or 'check by inspection', the check is good to a few degrees only. Star map: right ascension 0 h is at the image centre and right ascension increases to the left; declination +90 degrees is at the top. For right ascension A and declination D in degrees: u = 0.5 - A / 360 (modulo 1, from the left edge), v = (90 - D) / 180 (from the top edge). Coverage: 'partial' means that a large part of the surface has no image data. In most of these files that part is black (21 to 68 percent of the surface); Deimos has light grey blank areas instead. The maps of Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are the exception: the build fills their areas with no image data (7 to 31 percent of the surface) with a zonal mean colour, and the fields latitudeLimitsDeg, filledBands and filledSharePercent describe the fill. filledSharePercent is the filled share of the surface of a sphere. A map with 'global' coverage can still have small black gaps (4.2 percent of the surface or less in these files); the note of the entry describes them. latitudeLimitsDeg gives [south, north]: the map has image data only between these two latitudes. For Jupiter the source itself fills the areas beyond these limits with a flat colour. colour: 'natural' = the source calls the image natural colour; 'near natural' = the image comes from filters for visible light, but it is not an exact copy of what the eye sees; 'enhanced' = false colour (the image uses light that the eye cannot see, or it makes colour differences stronger); 'grey' = one filter only. An entry with no colour field has no such class in this work. The fields filters and observed come from the source. Ring strip: the left edge is at innerRadiusKm and the right edge is at outerRadiusKm from the centre of the planet. The radius is linear along the strip. See the note of the entry saturn_ring.

textures.note: Hubble Space Telescope map of 29 August 2025 (OPAL programme). The source page calls this file 'RotA Color Preview'. The readme gives for the first rotation: 'Rotation 1 (Aug 29 05:53:28 to 14:20:17 UT)'. Clouds change with time. The readme says: 'Color maps (TIFF only), are generated from the F631N (red), F502N (green), and F395N (blue) filters, with slight contrast enhancement.' So the colour is near natural, not exact: the blue channel is violet light of 395 nm. The latitude is planetographic (readme: 'between -90 and +90 deg planetographic latitude', with 'equatorial and polar radii of 60268 and 54364 km'). With these radii the planetographic latitude is larger than the planetocentric latitude by up to 5.9 degrees. The source removes the limb darkening of each image (readme: 'Minnaert correction'). So the map has no day side and no night side. The readme says: 'seams between maps were interpolated to smooth, where needed' and 'ARTIFACTS: Multiple moons (and their shadows) can be seen crossing the mosaics.' The original file has no image data near the poles and in a band near the equator: these areas are black, and each has a dark ragged border. The readme does not explain the band near the equator. My reading: the rings and their shadow hide the planet there. The build treats the borders as no data too. So the image data cover 75.2 degrees north to 82.2 degrees south, without the band from 5.4 degrees north to 0.6 degrees south. The build fills the rest (7.4 percent of the surface of a sphere): see the fields latitudeLimitsDeg and filledBands. The fill is not an observation. Inspection of the small image: the map shows pale bands. They are pink-grey in the north, bright yellow-white at the equator and green-grey in the south. A blue-grey band lies near 67 degrees south. The valid rows get darker and browner toward both limits, so the fill at both poles is brown. My reading: these rows lie near the edge of the disc in the Hubble images. A faint red-brown vertical stripe lies at about 17 percent of the width, mostly in the north. My reading: it is a seam between two images of the source. A faint red-brown smudge remains at this place at both fill limits. The map has a few small dark dots and bright dots (moons and their shadows, by the readme). No seam is visible at the left and right edge: the two edges differ by 1 of 255 on average. The original file has 1800 x 900 pixels (5 pixels per degree): the published image is not sharper than the original.

textures.note: PNG with transparency (straight alpha, not premultiplied). The horizontal axis is the distance from the centre of Saturn: the left edge is at 74,658 km (inner edge of the C ring) and the right edge is at 136,780 km (outer edge of the A ring). The radius is linear along the strip (30.33 km per pixel). All rows are equal. The strip comes from a Cassini mosaic of 12 December 2004 (PIA06175). The caption says: 'This mosaic of six images covers a distance of approximately 62,000 kilometers along the ring plane, from a radius of 74,565 kilometers to 136,780 kilometers (46,333 to 84,991 miles) from the planet's center.' and 'This view is from Cassini's vantage point beneath the ring plane. The rings are tilted away from Cassini at an angle of about 4 degrees.' and 'Images taken using red, green and blue spectral filters were used to create this natural color mosaic.' Alpha is the brightness of the image and not a measured opacity (field alphaSource). The colour of each pixel times its alpha value gives the brightness of the image again. The colour is a mean over 9 columns of the image (field colourSource): in the image the blue channel is less sharp than the red and green channels, and this makes colour fringes at sharp ring edges. Inspection of the strip: it shows the C ring (alpha about 0.1 to 0.5), the B ring (0.6 to 0.95), the Cassini division (0.05 to 0.6) and the A ring (0.5 to 0.65) with the Encke gap and the Keeler gap. The colour is warm tan in the B ring, pale pink in the A ring and lavender in the C ring and in the Cassini division: the image has these colours. The gaps are not fully clear: their alpha is 0.02 to 0.05. The image has a brightness of 5 to 9 of 255 in the gaps and of 1 to 3 in the sky just outside of the A ring. My reading: this is stray light. The caption does not say which face of the rings the image shows. The dense B ring is the brightest part of the image. So my reading is: the image shows the sunlit face. The strip has no D ring and no F ring: the image does not show them. Radius scale: the build fits a straight line to five sharp ring edges of the fact sheet (field radiusFit). These five edges agree with the fit to 5 km. Three other features differ from the fact sheet by 45 km to 88 km: the inner edge of the Maxwell ringlet, the inner edge of the B ring (a slow rise in the image) and the inner edge of the A ring (a small step in the image). So a ring feature can lie up to about 90 km (3 pixels) from its true place. The fit gives 10.87 km per pixel of the original image. The caption says: 'The image scale is 10.5 kilometers (6.5 miles) per pixel.' By the fit the image starts at 74,699 km. So the first pixel of the large strip has no image data: its alpha value is 0.

The rows near both poles are smeared. The map has no black area. The original has scattered single black pixels with the value 0 (0.06 percent of its pixels). My reading: they have no data. Its last column has 272 of them and its first column has 83: after a plain resize they make a thin dark broken line at the left and right edge. So the build fills these pixels in the first 8 and the last 8 columns (582 pixels): see the field changes. After this repair no seam is visible at the left and right edge. The file is the browse image (8-bit PNG) of the data file eros_nearmsi_filter4.tif (32-bit). The archive does not say how it scales the values to 8 bits. The projection uses a sphere of 17 km radius. Eros is very far from a sphere: the map does not fit a sphere. The original file has 10682 x 5341 pixels (10 m per pixel).
